title: CERN Wants to Drop Atoms Down a Shaft
hook: A 100-metre vertical atom interferometer in an LHC access shaft would hunt ultralight dark matter in a mass range nothing else can reach — and listen for gravitational waves below LIGO's floor.
key_points: AICE is a proposed ~100 m vertical atom interferometer in the PX46 access shaft at CERN.
Primary goal: search for bosonic ultralight dark matter in a mass range inaccessible to other experiments.
Secondary goal: pioneer gravitational-wave detection at 0.03–3 Hz, below the band ground-based detectors cover.
It works by interfering ultracold strontium-87 atoms in a multi-source gradiometer; swapping isotopes changes what it is sensitive to.
The proposal reports no technical showstoppers and 57 institutions across 22 countries behind it.
content_html: Atom interferometry does to matter what a laser interferometer does to light: split a cloud of ultracold atoms into two quantum paths, let them fall, and recombine them. The interference pattern records anything that nudged the two paths differently — including, potentially, a passing dark-matter field or a gravitational wave. Make the baseline longer and the sensitivity grows, which is why CERN is eyeing a very deep hole.
extra_html: The AICE technical proposal describes a roughly 100-metre vertical interferometer installed against the wall of PX46, an access shaft to the LHC. Three atom sources along the shaft form a gradiometer, with a fourth at the surface for laser stabilisation. Ultracold strontium-87 in a single-photon 698 nm interferometer targets scalar ultralight dark matter; running strontium-88 instead opens up axion-like particles, vector dark matter with B−L couplings, and tests of the equivalence principle, with a ytterbium-171 upgrade to follow. The secondary science case is gravitational waves at 0.03–3 Hz, below what ground-based detectors reach, as a pathfinder for longer baselines. The collaboration — 57 institutions in 22 countries, building on the VLBAI, MAGIS and AION-10 efforts — reports that PX46 is implementation-ready with no technical showstoppers, and that site preparation during the next long shutdown would let AICE run without disturbing the HL-LHC.

related.title: A Quantum Sensor Built to Catch Dark Matter and Ancient Gravitational Waves
related.hook: Two clouds of ultracold atoms, compared against each other, cancel out noise so well that a signal buried in one measurement reappears — aimed at dark matter and ancient gravitational waves.

related.title: A Dark Matter Detector That Asks Which Way the Hit Came From
related.hook: Neutrons and dark matter can leave identical-looking recoils. MIMAC's answer: reconstruct the direction of each recoil and check whether it points where dark matter should come from.

related.title: Gravitational Waves: Ripples in Spacetime
related.hook: When black holes collide, they shake the fabric of spacetime itself, sending out ripples that stretch and squeeze everything they pass — by less than the width of a proton.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

flashcards.prompt: What is AICE's primary scientific target?
flashcards.back_html: Bosonic ultralight dark matter — in a mass range that other experiments cannot reach. Gravitational waves at 0.03–3 Hz are the secondary goal.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the 0.03–3 Hz gravitational-wave band interesting for a new detector?

choices.text: It sits below the band ground-based detectors like LIGO cover
It is where the loudest black-hole mergers happen
It is the only band where general relativity can be tested

flashcards.explanation_html: AICE is framed as a pathfinder for longer-baseline detectors in this low-frequency range, which existing ground-based interferometers do not reach.

flashcards.prompt: How does changing the atomic species change what AICE can look for?
flashcards.back_html: The baseline uses ultracold strontium-87 for scalar ultralight dark matter. Strontium-88 adds sensitivity to axion-like particles, vector dark matter with B−L couplings, and equivalence-principle violation; a ytterbium-171 upgrade sharpens those.
